You are reviewing PR #79 in the ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa repo (a Salesforce PWA Kit storefront) for code conventions and structure, as part of a senior engineer's PR review. Fresh, independent pass — report exactly what you find, don't assume prior findings.

Get the live diff: `gh pr diff 79` in /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa. The PR touches exactly two files:
- overrides/app/ssr/contentSecurityPolicy.ts (Tier 1 SSR config)
- overrides/app/components/_app-config/index.tsx (Tier 2 Global Shell component, mounted on every page)

It implements per-request nonce-based CSP for `style-src` (splitting it into `style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr`), wiring the nonce from a new `getOrCreateNonce` helper in `contentSecurityPolicy.ts` through `res.locals` into `_app-config`, which uses it to configure an `@emotion/react` `CacheProvider`.

Read this repo's own written conventions before judging anything — do not apply generic best practice, apply THIS repo's house rules:
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/rules/conventions.md (naming, imports, DRY/KISS/SOLID, magic numbers/strings, no console.log, Australian spelling in Zimmermann-authored code — note override files keep upstream spelling verbatim)
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/rules/typescript.md (any/type vs interface, non-null assertions, discriminated unions, utility types, import type, satisfies vs as, readonly, generic naming)
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/rules/components.md (JSDoc requirements: required on any exported hook and any utility function with non-obvious behaviour; component/prop-type placement rules — note: this PR does not add a new component or hook per se, `getOrCreateNonce` is a module-private const in an SSR config file, so judge whether component.md's JSDoc bar for "utility function with non-obvious behaviour" should reasonably extend to it, given it already HAS a JSDoc comment — assess whether that JSDoc is actually good, not whether one exists)
- AGENTS.md's top-level rules (TypeScript-only in overrides/, minimal-changes principle, no refactoring upward, no renaming/moving shared hooks)

Already confirmed by someone else, so do not re-flag these as new findings:
- `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run lint`, `npm run test`, `node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs` are byte-for-byte identical between this PR's head and develop base — zero new violations on any of the four. (You don't need to re-run these.)
- No test file was added or modified by this PR (confirmed: `gh pr diff 79 --name-only` shows only the two files above). This is being tracked separately as a possible should-fix (missing unit test for the new `getOrCreateNonce` memoization logic) — you don't need to re-raise it, but feel free to weigh in on whether you agree it warrants a test given this repo's testing.md philosophy ("write tests where failure would be non-obvious or costly to debug... pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken").
- The `ChakraProvider` import on line 8 of `_app-config/index.tsx` is pre-existing/unchanged by this diff, not a new violation.

YOUR JOB — a structure and convention pass on the two changed files:
1. Comment quality and density: this PR's comments are unusually long and detailed (multi-paragraph explanations inline in the source). Is this appropriate given conventions.md's "default to no comments, only when the WHY is non-obvious" bar, or has it tipped into over-documentation that would be better placed in the PR description/a doc rather than inline? Give a real judgment, not a reflexive "more comments bad."
2. Naming: `CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`, `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY`, `getOrCreateNonce`, `ResponseWithLocals`, `emotionCache` — do these follow this repo's naming conventions (camelCase for Zimmermann-authored code, magic-string/number extraction requirement)?
3. TypeScript idioms: the `ResponseWithLocals = ServerResponse & { locals: Record<string, unknown> }` type and the cast `res as ResponseWithLocals` — is this the right escape hatch per typescript.md's rules on `any`/assertions (must have inline comment explaining why — it does; judge whether the explanation is actually sound)? Is `Record<string, unknown>` for `.locals` appropriately narrow, or could/should it be typed more precisely given `AppLocals` already exists as a shape in `_app-config/index.tsx`? Any place a `type` vs `interface` or `readonly` call was made that's worth a second look?
4. Whether `getOrCreateNonce` and the `ResponseWithLocals` type belong in this SSR config file at all, or whether the "no refactoring upward" / single-responsibility principle suggests they're doing too much for a file whose existing job was just exporting a static config object — is this scope creep within the file, or a reasonable minimal addition?
5. Whether AppLocals' new optional `cspNonce?: string` field and its placement/documentation matches how the rest of that type's fields are documented in the same file.
6. Any commented-out code, leftover debug statements, or console.log/console.error calls introduced (should be none, but verify).
7. Anything else structurally worth flagging — but skip pure taste preferences with no rule behind them.

Report a plain list of findings: what you found, file:line, which specific rule/doc section it maps to (or "no rule violated, just a judgment call" if that's the honest answer), and your confidence. If the comment density question in point 1 is your only real finding, that's a fine, complete result — don't manufacture additional nitpicks to pad the list.

content.text:
## PR #79 Review Findings — Code Conventions & Structure

Reviewed against the live diff (`gh pr diff 79`) and the actual PR head commit (`8a6162750e`, branch `fix/SFCC-856-csp-hardening-v2`). Line numbers below are from that head commit. I independently verified the diff's own factual claims against the actual installed packages and SDK source rather than taking the comments at face value — details noted where relevant.

---

**1. Comment density — real judgment, not reflexive**

Roughly 84 of the 132 added lines (~64%) are comment-only. That's a genuinely high ratio, but I checked whether the density is padding or substance by independently verifying nearly every non-obvious factual claim made in these comments:

- helmet 4.6.0's `(req, res) => string` CSP directive-function signature (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:7-14`) — confirmed against `node_modules/helmet/dist/middlewares/content-security-policy/index.d.ts` and the installed version (4.6.0). Accurate.
- The `strictFunctionTypes` assignability reasoning (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:16-24`) — confirmed `tsconfig.json` has `strict: true`, and worked through the variance rule by hand: a call signature (not method-shorthand) is checked contravariantly, so narrowing `res`'s parameter type to `ResponseWithLocals` would indeed break assignability to helmet's declared type. Sound.
- `res.locals` being the same object passed as `AppConfig`'s `locals` prop — confirmed in `node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk/ssr/server/react-rendering.js:317-318` (`React.createElement(AppConfig, {locals: res.locals})`). Accurate.
- The client's fresh/empty `locals` object — confirmed in `node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-react-sdk/ssr/browser/main.js:101-107` verbatim. Accurate (the comment cites the file as `main.jsx`; the real file is `main.js` — trivial, doesn't affect anything, mentioning only for completeness).
- The `sha256-GNF74DLkXb0fH3ILHgILFjk1ozCF3SNXQ5mQb7WLu/Y=` hash (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:118`) — recomputed independently from the actual `preventTransition()` string in `node_modules/@chakra-ui/color-mode/dist/color-mode.utils.js`. Byte-for-byte match.
- `react-helmet`'s ambient declaration already existing — confirmed in `overrides/app/types/vendor.d.ts:138-153`.

Given the subject matter (CSP is unforgiving — a wrong value fails silently until a browser blocks something in production) and that this is verifiably accurate, hard-won information (the sprite-sheet and `preventTransition()` bugs were apparently found live on MRT preview, per the PR body), I don't think this is over-documentation in the "explaining the obvious" sense conventions.md would object to. It's dense because the underlying interaction (CSP3 spec nuance + a third-party package's non-React DOM write + a TypeScript variance rule) is dense, not because the author padded it.

That said, two spots are genuinely disproportionate and could be trimmed without losing anything:
- `_app-config/index.tsx:102-107` — the `cspNonce?: string` field gets a 5-line comment; every sibling field in the same `AppLocals` type (`appConfig`, `site`, `locale`, `buildUrl`, `originalUrl`) has zero inline comment. A 1-2 line version pointing to the fuller explanation already given at `CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`'s declaration (lines 53-59) would match the surrounding file convention better.
- `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:29-39` — `getOrCreateNonce`'s JSDoc re-explains the same `res.locals` → `AppConfig` prop pass-through story already told in the comment block immediately above it (lines 7-24), two declarations earlier in the same file. This is direct, adjacent redundancy, not just "a lot of comments" — a tighter JSDoc describing the function's own contract (idempotent, caches on first call, returns a base64 nonce) with a pointer to the block above for the cross-file architecture would remove the duplication.

No rule in `conventions.md` sets an explicit comment-density ceiling (I checked — the closest stated rule is the commented-out-code rule, which is a different concern), so this is a judgment call, but a well-evidenced one: mostly justified, with two concrete, fixable instances of redundancy rather than a blanket problem.

**2. Naming**

`CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`, `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY`, `getOrCreateNonce`, `ResponseWithLocals`, `emotionCache` are all correctly cased (SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants, PascalCase types, camelCase functions/variables) and consistent with established precedent in the same directory — `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` already uses `CLAIM`/`DELIMITER` SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants for the exact same magic-string-extraction purpose, and `_app-config/index.tsx` already imports SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants like `STORE_LOCATOR_RADIUS`/`DEFAULT_DNT_STATE`. No violation, high confidence.

One thing worth a second look, low-to-moderate confidence, no clean rule citation: the sha256 hash at `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:118` is a raw string literal inline in the `style-src-elem` array, not hoisted to a named constant the way `CSP_NONCE_META_NAME`/`CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY` were — despite having a whole paragraph next to it explaining it's fragile and needs manual recomputation on a Chakra bump. conventions.md's magic-string rule would seem to favor a named constant here (e.g. `CHAKRA_PREVENT_TRANSITION_STYLE_HASH`). Counter-argument: every other CSP directive value in this same file (`'self'`, `'unsafe-inline'`, `'*.stripe.com'`, etc.) is also a bare inline literal — the file's own established pattern treats directive arrays as literal-value lists, not constant references — so the hash is arguably consistent with that existing local convention rather than a deviation. I'd call this genuinely arguable rather than a clear violation.

Separately: `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY = 'cspNonce'` (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:27`, written via bracket access) and `AppLocals.cspNonce` (`_app-config/index.tsx:107`, read via dot access) both spell `cspNonce`, but nothing mechanically links them — one is a runtime string constant, the other is a hardcoded property name in a type in a completely different file. Renaming `CSP_NONCE_LOCALS_KEY`'s value alone wouldn't produce a compile error; it would just silently make `locals.cspNonce` always `undefined`, which would only surface as a live CSP violation in a browser, not in `tsc`/tests. Low confidence this is worth fixing (both files cross-reference each other by name in comments, so the practical drift risk is low), but it's a real, if narrow, gap — no shared source of truth for the key name across the two files.

**3. TypeScript idioms**

- `type ResponseWithLocals = ServerResponse & { locals: Record<string, unknown> }` (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:25`) and the cast `res as ResponseWithLocals` (line 41) — this is the correct escape hatch per typescript.md, and the inline comment pointing back to the fuller explanation is sound, not just present. I verified the underlying reasoning myself (see point 1) rather than taking the comment on faith, and it holds up: the parameter must stay typed as the plain `ServerResponse` helmet declares, so the cast has to happen inside the function body. Good design choice, too — the cast is encapsulated once inside `getOrCreateNonce` rather than pushed onto every call site.
- `Record<string, unknown>` for `.locals`, then narrowing via `typeof existing === 'string'` — this is a textbook-correct application of typescript.md's own guidance ("Prefer `unknown` with a type guard when the shape is genuinely not known at that point"). I don't think `AppLocals` should be reused here even though it exists: `AppLocals` describes the fully-populated shape as seen by the React `AppConfig` component *after* `AppConfig.restore()` runs; `contentSecurityPolicy.ts` operates earlier, at the Express/helmet middleware layer, before that population happens, and only ever touches one key. Importing a Tier 2 component file's local type into a Tier 1 SSR config file would also be a backwards dependency direction. Reasonable as-is, high confidence.
- `type` (not `interface`) for `ResponseWithLocals` — correct per typescript.md's default preference, and consistent with why the sibling `overrides/app/ssr/types.ts` deviates to `interface` for `SsrRes` (explicitly commented there: "`this` return type requires interface... for polymorphic self-type") — that reason doesn't apply here, so `type` is the right call.
- `readonly` — not applicable anywhere in this diff; `.locals` is deliberately mutated (nonce caching), so `readonly` would be wrong there, and correctly wasn't used.
- `import type { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http'` — correctly type-only; `randomBytes`, `CacheProvider`, `createCache`, `Helmet` are all correctly plain (value) imports since they're used at runtime. No misapplication either direction.

**4. Does `getOrCreateNonce`/`ResponseWithLocals` belong in this file?**

The function itself: yes, and I think this is closer to "the only viable place" than "reasonable minimal addition." `overrides/app/ssr.js` is absolutely frozen under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4 (no exception, unlike other Tier 1 files), and helmet's directive-value-as-function mechanism means the nonce logic can only live inside the config object `ssr.js` imports — i.e., this file. Not scope creep; it's the CSP policy's own implementation detail.

The type: more genuinely a judgment call. `overrides/app/ssr/types.ts` exists specifically for "minimal structural types for SSR Express handlers" to avoid a hard `@types/express` dependency, and every other sibling file that needs Express-adjacent types (`slasTokens.ts`, `marketingCloud.ts`, `paymentMetadata.ts` — 3 of 4 siblings) imports `SsrReq`/`SsrRes` from there rather than declaring locally. `ResponseWithLocals` is conceptually the same category of thing and currently duplicates that file's reason for existing, one level over. On the other hand: it has exactly one consumer today (conventions.md's DRY guidance says extract "once the same pattern appears in two places," not preemptively), and it's built differently from `types.ts`'s existing types — it intersects with the real Node `http.ServerResponse` rather than being a fully independent structural interface, because it has to satisfy helmet's exact declared function type under `strictFunctionTypes`. Moving it would mean introducing an `http` import into a file that currently has none and mixing two different typing strategies there. I'd call this a legitimate "worth a second look" rather than a rule violation in either direction.

**5. `AppLocals.cspNonce?: string` placement/documentation**

Placement (`_app-config/index.tsx:107`, appended after `originalUrl?`) matches convention — all fields are optional with bare `?`, new field added at the end, same style. Comment length does not match convention — see point 1's first bullet; every sibling field in this type has zero comment, `cspNonce` gets five lines. The imbalance is explainable (this is the one field whose value doesn't originate from `AppConfig.restore()` in this same file, unlike its siblings), but proportionally it stands out, and could be trimmed.

**6. console.log / debug statements / commented-out code**

None found. I grepped every added line (`+` in the diff) for `console.`, `debugger`, `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX` — the only match is inside a comment documenting a maintenance command (`` `node -e "console.log(...)"` `` at `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:117`, a recipe for recomputing the hash if Chakra changes), not an actual runtime `console.log` call. I also re-read every added comment block manually; all are prose explanations, none are disabled/commented-out code. Clean.

**7. Other findings**

- `@emotion/cache` (`_app-config/index.tsx:10`) is imported for the first time anywhere in this codebase, and — like `@emotion/react` and `react-helmet`, both already used elsewhere (`overrides/app/theme/fontFace.tsx`, `overrides/app/theme/zimmTokensGlobal.tsx`, `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx`) — it's not declared in root `package.json` at all; it resolves only because it's a transitive dependency of the already-used `@emotion/react`. This isn't a new pattern this PR introduces (the same "undeclared transitive dependency" situation already exists for `@emotion/react` itself in Tier 1 theme files), and no `package.json`/lockfile edit occurred, so I don't think Hard Rule #7 is actually implicated — flagging only because it's the kind of thing that could break silently on an unrelated dependency-tree reshuffle. Low confidence this needs action; mentioning for completeness only.
- On the separately-tracked missing-test question: I agree it's a defensible should-fix, not a must-fix, under testing.md's own bar. `getOrCreateNonce`'s caching branch (return existing vs. generate-and-store) is exactly "pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken" — a regression there (e.g., losing the cache-and-reuse behavior, or generating a nonce that doesn't match between the header and the meta tag) wouldn't be caught by `tsc`, lint, or any existing test, only by a live CSP violation. That said, testing it requires mocking a `ServerResponse`-shaped object, which is minor friction, not a blocker. I'd weigh it the same way the tracked item does: worth adding, not worth blocking on.

**Not flagged, considered and ruled out:** repeated literal directive values (`'self'`, `'unsafe-inline'`, `'static.client.measmerize.com'`) across `style-src`/`style-src-elem`/`style-src-attr` — this matches the file's own pre-existing, unchanged convention of repeating origin strings across directives (`'*.stripe.com'` etc. already repeat across `script-src`/`connect-src`/`frame-src`), so holding the new code to a stricter DRY standard than the rest of the file wasn't consistent. Also ruled out: forward-referencing `isServerSide` (declared at line 266) from inside `cspNonce`'s resolution at line 161 — safe, since `AppConfig` the function isn't invoked until after full module evaluation completes; not a TDZ bug.
